<div class="callout-note">
**About this guide**
I show you how to access UdeSherbrooke's iv12 (aka Mammouth) supercomputer. This node is only accessible to UdS students and requires DRAC sponsorship.

This tutorial is tailored for members of the [Laforest Lab](https://www.laforestlab.com/), so some variables or definitions might need to be changed if you are in a different lab.
</div>

<div class="callout-danger">
As of summer 2026, iv12 (formerly ip34) is accessible via a **login node** where no computation of any kind is allowed. All actual work happens on `cv3401`, a large dedicated compute node you need to access once you are logged in. Essentially, you log into `hpc-bio.ccs.usherbrooke.ca`, then connect to `cv3401` before doing anything else.
</div>

---
Steps 1, 2 and 4 only need to be done once.
---

# Create a DRAC account

To work on ip34, you need a [Digital Research Alliance of Canada](https://ccdb.alliancecan.ca/security/login) account. Ask your director for their sponsorship code. For help, visit their [FAQ](https://docs.alliancecan.ca/wiki/Frequently_Asked_Questions_about_the_CCDB/fr).

---

# Initial setup (locally) 

You only need to do this once, forever!

## Local configuration {.tabset}
This will periodically send a signal to Mammouth to make sure you don't spontaneously get logged out. _You only need to do this once._

### On a Mac

Open the Terminal app and run the following:

```{bash mac-ssh}
touch ~/.ssh/config
echo "Host *" >> ~/.ssh/config
echo ServerAliveInterval 60 >> ~/.ssh/config
```


### On Windows

1. Navigate to the `.ssh` program in your home folder, typically under `C:\Users:\<username>\.ssh`
2. Open the config file; if there is none, right-click inside the .ssh folder and select New > Text Document
3. Add the following lines to the file:

```
Host iv12.ccs.usherbrooke.ca
    ServerAliveInterval 60
```

Save it and quit. Then, open the PowerShell app and execute the following command:

```
$env:TERM = "xterm-256color"
```


Then, proceed with the next steps.

## {-}

<div class="callout-note">
If you need a quick primer on the bash language syntax, which is the language the code blocks below are written in, checkout Mike Lee's [awesome tutorial](https://astrobiomike.github.io/unix/unix-intro).
</div>

## Setting up DUO 2FA

All alliance supercomputers require 2-factor authentification using the DUO app. Follow [these steps](https://docs.alliancecan.ca/wiki/Multifactor_authentication#Registering_factors) to set it up.

---

# Logging on to iv12

Whenever you want to access iv12, run this command with your DRAC username (will prompt for password; nothing shows when you'll write your password, that's normal!). Here, use the username to your DRAC account (not your email), for example:

```{bash login}
ssh username@iv12.ccs.usherbrooke.ca
```

<div class="callout-note">
**Note:** confirm this hostname with your lab/sysadmin if it doesn't resolve — it's the direct rename of the old `ip34.ccs.usherbrooke.ca` address, but double-check before relying on it.
</div>

You will be prompted with 2FA, which will look like:

```
Enter a passcode or select one of the following options:
1. Duo Push to Pixel8 (Android)
Passcode or option (1-1):
```

Type 1, press return, and you will receive a notification to approve on your phone.

Once you are logged in, you'll see something that looks like this (it might change)

```
######################################################################################

SVP ne lancez pas de calculs sur ce noeud, lancer plutôt un calul interactif.
Please do not launch your programs on this node, use interactive compute job instead:

salloc -p bio --time=3:00:00 --cpus-per-task=8 --mem=4gb

Vous pouvez rejoindre les anciens répertoires via.
You can reach old directories with:

/net/nfs-bio/

######################################################################################
```
When you see `>`at the bottom, that means Mammouth is ready to receive commands! (The exact banner text may differ slightly post-restructuring, but the cluster underneath — Mp2b — is the same.)

<div class="callout-danger">
**Remember: you are still on the login node (`iv12`) at this point.** Nothing computational runs here anymore — no `R`, no scripts, nothing that uses real CPU or memory. Keep reading to see how to reach `cv3401`, where you're actually allowed to work.
</div>

```bash
newgrp def-ilafores
```

<div class="callout-danger">
**Important: you must** execute that command **EVERY TIME** you log on!
</div>

Otherwise, any file you create will only be readable and writable by you. Do not add the newgrp command to your bashrc, tempting as it may be.

---

# Initial setup (iv12)

Add a few lines to your `.bashrc` file, which is executed every time you login.

<div class="callout-note">
This code block only needs to be executed **once**, ever!
</div>

```{bash bashrc}
# Sets up certain permissions: 
echo umask 007 >> ~/.bashrc

# Allows access to certain programs (e.g. cutadapt):
echo export MUGQIC_INSTALL_HOME=/cvmfs/soft.mugqic/CentOS6 >> ~/.bashrc 
echo 'module use $MUGQIC_INSTALL_HOME/modulefiles'  >> ~/.bashrc			

# Create a $ILAFORES variable:
echo export ILAFORES=/jbod2/def-ilafores >> ~/.bashrc

# add a little reminder ...
echo echo "REMINDER: change group id before working!" >> ~/.bashrc
echo echo "newgrp def-<your-PI-group-name>" >> ~/.bashrc

# Execute the .bashrc (happens every time you log in, but we need those variables now!)
source ~/.bashrc 

```

<div class="callout-note">
Each command with `>>` appends something to the `.bashrc` file. If you do them multiple times, you'll be adding multiple lines to it. `.bashrc` is a file that is executed each time you log in, so you can add more variable definitions to it, which we'll do below.
</div>

I suggest adding another variable to your `.bashrc` that will contain the path to your project directory, allowing you to move to that directory without having to type the full path every time.

In the following, replace `your_project_name` with the name you want your project directory to have, and `PROJECT1` by a short name you'll remember (it will create a variable pointing to your project directory path, which you can use in place of the path when using the command line).

```{bash project}
# Makes sure the variable exists whenever you log in:
echo "export PROJECT1=$ILAFORES/analysis/your_project_name" >> ~/.bashrc

# execute the bashrc:
source ~/.bashrc

# create your project directory:
mkdir -p $PROJECT1
```

Then, whenever you log in to iv12, using the project directory variable name you've chosen (here PROJECT1), all you have to do is

```{bash daily}
newgrp def-ilafores  # don't forget! ;-)
cd $PROJECT1
```

<div class="callout-note">
Check out [this cool tutorial](https://astrobiomike.github.io/unix/unix-intro) to learn how to get around a little more using this language (bash). Calcul Québec  also regularly give 3-hour workshops on command line (bash) programming for Linux. Check out [their offer](https://www.calculquebec.ca/services-aux-chercheurs/formation/catalogue/).
</div>

You are not ready to "do science" quite yet, though — you're still on `iv12`, and no computation is allowed here. Keep reading.

---

# What's next? {.tabset}

If you are working with amplicon data, next steps would be to

1. Setup your R environment and reach `cv3401` (below)
2. Follow [the DADA2 tutorial](https://jorondo1.github.io/mgx.tutorials/dada2_16S_tutorial.html)

## Setting up the R environment

In microbial ecology, when using R, many packages are often required. Packages are bundles of functions that make coding easier, developed by people like you and me around the world. Installing packages on iv12 can sometimes be a bit problematic, so we have a shared library you can copy into your environment and then build on top of it or update depending on your requirements. This is a one-time step, and it's just a file copy, so it's fine to run directly on `iv12`:

```{bash r-libs}
mkdir -p ~/R/x86_64-pc-linux-gnu-library/4.4
cp -r $ILAFORES/R_libs_20260401/* ~/R/x86_64-pc-linux-gnu-library/4.4
```

## Reaching `cv3401` with `tmux` + `salloc`

<div class="callout-danger">
**This is the step that replaces what used to be "just start R."** `iv12` cannot run R (or anything else that computes) anymore — everything happens on `cv3401`, the lab's shared compute node, reached with Slurm's `salloc`. The good news: once you're on `cv3401`, everything works exactly as it did before — same `module load`, same `nice R`, same interactive session, quality plots and all.
</div>

First, start a `tmux` session **on `iv12`**, so that a dropped connection (closed laptop, flaky wifi, going home for the day) doesn't kill your work — `tmux` keeps running on the server even if you disconnect. If you're new to `tmux`, it creates a virtual shell that persists in the background: close your terminal or log out, and whatever is running inside it keeps going.

```{bash tmux-new}
tmux new -s your_session_name
```

The text will disappear on your shell and a green line will appear at the bottom — you're in a tmux session. From **inside** this tmux session, request a slice of `cv3401`:

```{bash salloc}
salloc --time=08:00:00 --cpus-per-task=24 --mem=250G --partition bio
```

<details>
<summary>
What do these salloc flags mean?
</summary>

- `--time=08:00:00`: how long you're reserving the allocation for (here, a full working day). When this runs out, your session is killed, so pick something comfortable for what you're doing — but don't request days on end "just in case," see below.
- `--cpus-per-task=24`: number of cores reserved for you, matching the `ncores <- 24` used throughout the DADA2 tutorial.
- `--mem=250G`: memory reserved. `cv3401` has an enormous amount of RAM available (in the terabyte range), so this is a generous but still considerate slice — increase it if a specific step genuinely needs more.
- `--partition bio`: routes the request specifically to `cv3401` rather than some other node.

</details>

Once `salloc` grants the allocation, your prompt changes and you are now **on `cv3401`**. This is where actual computation is allowed. Load the R environment and start R exactly as before:

```{bash r-load}
module load StdEnv/2023 r/4.4.0 mugqic/cutadapt/2.10
nice R
```

<div class="callout-ip34">
`cv3401` is shared with the rest of the lab, so `salloc` is what keeps everyone's usage fair and visible — instead of everyone informally self-limiting on a shared login node, Slurm now enforces it by only ever giving you the slice you asked for. Still be considerate: don't request more cores/memory/time than you need, and release your allocation (see below) as soon as you're done rather than leaving it idle.
</div>

<details>
<summary>
what's nice?
</summary>
`nice` is recommended so your program is "nice to others" sharing the same allocation logic. Once you run this, you are in the equivalent of an R console, which accepts R commands (don't write in bash!). The `>` at the beginning of a new line expects commands in the R language. You'll need to install the packages you need (only once), as you once did on your computer. By default, your current directory will be the one you were in when you activated R.
</details>

### Detaching, reattaching, and cleaning up

You can detach from `tmux` (leaving both `tmux` and your `salloc` allocation running) with `Ctrl+B` then `D`. You'll land back on `iv12`. Check what's still running with:

```{bash tmux-ls}
tmux ls
```

Reattach to it later with:

```{bash tmux-attach}
tmux attach -t your_session_name
```

...and you'll find your R session on `cv3401` exactly as you left it, as long as your `--time` allocation hasn't expired.

<div class="callout-danger">
**When you're actually done for the day**, don't just detach — quit R with `q()`, then `exit` the `salloc` shell to release your allocation. Otherwise you keep holding 24 cores and 250 GB idle until the time limit runs out, unavailable to your labmates.
</div>

<div class="callout-note">
To learn more about tmux (like how to see multiple sessions simultaneously), check out [this blog post](https://www.redhat.com/en/blog/introduction-tmux-linux).
</div>
# {-}


# Visualizing output files locally

When you generate plots or other output files on ip34, you can't open them directly because there is no graphic interface. To view them, you need to **download them to your local computer** using `scp` (Secure Copy Protocol) or `rsync``. This is done from a **local terminal** (not from your ip34 session).

## Finding the path on ip34

First, you need the full path to the file or folder you want to download. In your ip34 session, navigate to the relevant directory and run:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
echo $PWD
```

This prints the absolute path to your current directory, e.g.:

```
/jbod2/def-ilafores/analysis/2026_MyProject/output_plots
```

<div class="callout-danger">
These are not R commands! You need access to a bash shell to do this. All the more reason to work with `tmux`, because now you can just detach from your session (`crtl+b`, then `d`); you'll land in your home session on ip34. There, you can run the command above to find the path to the desired output folder. 
</div>

## Downloading your files {.tabset}

This part needs to be done from a local shell, meaning a new shell that's not connected to ip34.

Generally, it looks like this (example with `scp`)

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
scp -r username@ip34.ccs.usherbrooke.ca:/path/to/source /path/to/local/destination
```

- `-r` copies directories recursively, so you don't have to point to individual files; you can copy the entire output directory and its content, e.g. `X_DADA_Summary` from the [improved DADA2 pipeline](https://jorondo1.github.io/mgx.tutorials/dada2_16S_tutorial.html).
- Replace `username` with your CCS username
- The part after `:` is the absolute path of the directory you want to copy, found with `echo $PWD`
- The second part is where on your computer you want these files copied

This command will prompt your for your ip34 password every time, including 2FA if applicable.

### On a Mac

Open a new Terminal window and run:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
rsync -avr username@ip34.ccs.usherbrooke.ca:/jbod2/def-ilafores/analysis/2026_MyProject/X_DADA_Summary ~/Documents/my_project/
```

`rsync` is available natively on Mac and will sync only files that have changed, making repeated transfers much faster.

### On Windows

Open a new PowerShell window and run:

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
scp -r username@ip34.ccs.usherbrooke.ca:/jbod2/def-ilafores/analysis/2026_MyProject/output_plots C:\Users\YourName\Documents\my_project\
```

<div class="callout-note">
**Tip:** To find the full path of a destination folder on Windows, right-click the folder, select **Properties**, and copy the path shown under **Location**. Windows paths use backslashes `\` and start with the drive letter (e.g. `C:`).
</div>
## {-}

<details>

<summary>
Save yourself time in the future...
</summary>

Once you've build your rsync or scp command, copy it somewhere so you don't have to do rewrite it or find the path to the source folder from within ip34 every time. I like to leave mine commented at the top of my R script.

</details>

Once the transfer completes, the files will be available locally and you can open them as usual.
